Contents

What the documentation and the forum say
Section 1: The slots the terminal sees
Section 2: What each slot accepts
Section 3: What the shift does to a real indicator
Section 4: IndicatorInputs.mqh, the mapper class
Section 5: The Strategy Tester

Using it in your own EA

Introduction
When an EA calls a custom indicator through iCustom() or IndicatorCreate(), it must pass the inputs in the order the terminal expects. If the indicator uses input groups, that order differs from the one in the inputs dialog. Each group line takes a slot of its own. In my tests on builds 6204 and 6230, the terminal accepted a shifted list of numeric values without any error. The CIndicatorInputs class reads the slot order from a running indicator instance. You set each value by its input number. The class fills the group slots and, on a chart, reads the created handle back to check every value. In the Strategy Tester the terminal does not report the order. There the class builds the handle from a layout file saved on a chart, and that handle stays unverified.
BandsLite, the small bands indicator attached to this article, has four inputs in two groups. I called it with iCustom(..., 50, 2.5, 3, 80.0), the way the parameter list of iCustom() suggests. The handle was valid and nothing appeared in the journal. The indicator received a period of 2, a deviation of 3.0, and the defaults for the other two inputs. Over 4,577 bars of EURUSD H1 in 2026, the intended settings gave 32 signals and the call I actually wrote gave 0. An EA built on that call would compile, load, and run without ever opening a trade.
The article measures the problem first and then builds the class. It covers which values each slot accepts through both functions, including negative, out-of-range, and non-finite values. It also covers a Strategy Tester restriction and how the class works around it. There are 61 unit tests, a tester EA, and a Python script that repeats the main calculations as a consistency check.
This is Part 1 of a series on MQL5 code that compiles and runs but quietly does something other than what it says.
What the documentation and the forum say
The
Input Variables
page describes input groups as a way to visually separate parameters in the inputs dialog. The same page says that iCustom() parameters "should go in a strict accordance with the declaration of input variables" of the indicator. The
iCustom()
page says the type and order of the parameters must match. Neither page says that a group line takes a place in that order.
The forum found it anyway. In January 2024 a user reported the behavior as
a bug with input group and iCustom()
, with sample code, on build 4150. A few days later Dominik Egert wrote in the
documentation errors thread
that the terminal handles group lines as regular inputs, and that each one has to be passed as an empty string. In May 2025 Robert Northen asked
whether input group affects the parameter array of IndicatorCreate()
and confirmed that three inputs under two group lines need five MqlParam entries. He asked MetaQuotes to put the rule in the documentation, and the pages above still don't mention it.
So the rule itself is known to people who read the forum, and anyone can count the group lines by hand. Counting by hand needs the source code, however, and the count breaks quietly the day the author adds a group. I could not find a class that reads the layout from a running indicator. I also found no measurement of when the shift fails with an error and when it stays silent, and nothing that covered the Strategy Tester. Those three points are what this article adds.
Section 1: The slots the terminal sees
IndicatorParameters() returns the parameters of an indicator handle as an array of MqlParam. For a custom indicator the first entry is the file name, and one entry follows for every slot. I created a BandsLite handle with no parameters, so it ran with its defaults, and printed what came back. The group lines are there as strings of the form "@group 'Name'", in the same places as in the source. In the output, IcustomGroups\BandsLite is a path. IcustomGroups is the project folder under MQL5\Indicators, not a misspelling of iCustom().

This is the layout the class works from. The slot numbers are what IndicatorCreate() and iCustom() count. The input numbers are what a person counts when reading the inputs dialog. Each group line above an input adds 1 to the gap between the two numbers.
Group lines are not the only extra slots. An indicator written with the short form of OnCalculate(), the one that receives a single price array, has an extra slot at the end for the applied price. InputEcho, the second test indicator, has five inputs in three groups and reports nine slots for that reason. SlotProbe, a third attached indicator, starts with an sinput variable and then has an empty group line. Both took a slot of their own, and the unit tests below set the sinput through the class like any other input.
The types in the reply are not always the declared ones. TypeSlots, the indicator used for the type tests in Section 2, has one group line and one input of each common type, followed by four narrower types. On build 6230 the reply described it like this:

Section 2: What each slot accepts

Within these 72 cells, three rules describe every result. A group slot accepts any value and keeps its own text. A string slot accepts only a string. Every other slot accepts any number and never a string. Along the way the fraction of a double is dropped in an integer slot, so 2.5 becomes 2 without a word. Any number other than 0 becomes true in a bool slot.

No edge value was refused, so the three rules about what loads still held. The stored values follow the usual C conversions. Integers wrap around, a double loses its fraction toward zero, and a double outside the int range becomes -2147483648. The bool 0.4 case was unexpected, since the value became true instead of losing its fraction and becoming 0. The terminal does not check an enum against its list, so 99 reached the indicator as a value the enum does not declare. Two results change values without any error: a float slot rounds to float precision, and a string slot keeps only the first 245 characters. TypeSlots writes the length of the string it received into a buffer, so the 245 is what the indicator itself saw, not only what IndicatorParameters() reported.
These rules cover the values in the two tables and nothing more. I did not test char, ushort, long, or ulong slots, and I did not try strings with characters outside the Latin range in a matrix cell.
What do the tables say about errors? Within this test set the terminal refused a handle only when a string met a numeric slot or a number met a string slot, with error 4002. So a shifted call to an indicator whose inputs are all numbers never produced 4002 here. A handle can still fail for reasons outside the matrix, such as a missing symbol, missing history, or a missing indicator file. A check inside the indicator's own OnInit() does not even make the handle invalid. NeedsInputs, attached for that case, refuses to start with its default period of 0. Its handle was valid, and BarsCalculated() stayed at -1.
The unit tests also checked a value placed past the last slot. A 7th value of 1 for BandsLite, which has six slots, was dropped and the handle loaded. A 7th value of 99 failed in both functions with error 4804, ERR_INDICATOR_CANNOT_APPLY. The terminal seems to read that position as the data source of the indicator, a price type or the handle of another indicator. I did not test that reading further.
Section 3: What the shift does to a real indicator
BandsLite is a plain Bollinger-style indicator. It draws a simple moving average with bands a number of standard deviations away. It marks a signal when price closes back inside after a number of closes outside. Figure 1 shows where the four values of the plain call end up, and where the same values end up with a placeholder in each group slot.
Where the values of iCustom(..., 50, 2.5, 3, 80.0) land

The 0 comes from the period of 2. With two closes, each close sits exactly 1 standard deviation from their mean. A band 3 deviations from the mean can never be crossed, so BandsLite with these inputs can never give a signal on any symbol. The bands are also far narrower and follow every bar. Figure 2 shows 150 bars in July.
EURUSD H1, 16 to 27 July 2026
The same indicator with the intended inputs and with the inputs the plain call delivered
Fig. 2. The intended bands stay wide and give 3 signals in these 150 bars, while the bands from the plain call hug the close and give none
Band width on every bar of 2026
EURUSD H1, 4,525 bars from 6 January, 100-point bins, 41 intended bars wider than 3,000 points not shown
Fig. 3. Most bands from the plain call are under 300 points wide, while the intended bands spread from about 300 to over 2,000 points
BandsLite is one example. When numeric inputs sit under group lines and the call passes no placeholders, the indicator runs with values nobody chose. A call with "" in each group slot does not have the problem. How visible the damage is depends on how far the shifted values are from the intended ones.
Section 4: IndicatorInputs.mqh, the mapper class
CIndicatorInputs takes the counting away from the caller. It reads the layout from the terminal and lets the caller set values by input number. It fills the group slots itself and checks the handle when it is created. Figure 4 shows the whole path, including the tester branch from Section 5.
How CIndicatorInputs builds a handle
On a chart or in a script the layout comes from the terminal. In the Strategy Tester it comes from a file.
Fig. 4. Load reads the slots, Probe sorts out groups and float inputs, Set checks each value, and Create builds the handle. On a chart Verify reads it back, while the tester reads a saved layout and skips the read-back

My first version decided which slots are groups by the text alone, a string value that starts with "@group '". That text format is not documented anywhere I could find. A regular string input whose default happens to start with the same text would also pass for a group. SlotProbe has such an input, and the text test counted three groups where there are two. So the text is now only a first guess. Probe() creates one more handle with a marker string in every string slot and 0.1 in every double slot. A group slot keeps its own text whatever it is given, which the matrix showed, while a string input takes the marker. A float input rounds 0.1 to 0.1000000015, which is how the class finds a float behind a DOUBLE type.

The probe rests on two observed behaviors, the group slot that keeps its text and the float rounding. A future build could change either one, and then the probe would sort the slots wrongly. PrefixMismatches() reports how many slots the text and the probe disagreed on, so a change in the group format at least shows up as a number.
Load() needs the indicator to be created with its defaults. NeedsInputs fails its own OnInit() with those defaults, and Load() still read all its slots, because the terminal creates the handle and reports the parameters even when the indicator refuses to calculate. However, NeedsInputs is a single case. An indicator whose handle can't be created at all, for example because the file is missing, can't be loaded.
The setters check the value against the slot before anything reaches the terminal. A number for a string input and a string for a numeric input are refused, since the terminal would answer with 4002 anyway. The other refusals cover the silent changes from the edge table. They refuse a fraction or an out-of-range number for an integer input, NaN and inf, a number beyond the float range for a float input, and a string over 245 characters.

Using it in your own EA
The change is small, and OnInit() of GroupCallerEA.mq5 in Section 5 shows the whole change. Replace the iCustom() call with a CIndicatorInputs object. Then set the values by input number, create the handle, and print LastError() if the handle comes back invalid.
Run Describe() once and compare it with the inputs dialog, so you know which input number is which. If the EA will be tested, run SaveLayout.mq5 for each indicator it calls, after every change to that indicator. Add a tester_file property for each layout file and load it with LoadLayout() when MQL_TESTER is set.
If you would rather not include the class, run SaveLayout.mq5 on the indicator and copy the line it prints. That line already has "" in every group slot. You then change the values in it by hand.
The class never opens the source file. IndicatorCreate() loads the compiled indicator, and IndicatorParameters() reads the slots from the running copy. Limitations
Everything here was measured on one terminal with MetaQuotes-Demo, first on build 6204 and again on build 6230. The main matrix and the tester runs gave the same results on both builds. The edge values, the reported types, the 245-character limit, and the 7th-value results come from build 6230 only.
Several results rest on behavior the documentation does not describe. They include the "@group '" text, the group slot that keeps its own text, the reported types, the float rounding, and the 245-character limit. A future build could change any of these. On a chart Verify() would then report a mismatch for a value that moved. However, a wrong group or float decision in Probe() can also shift the input numbers themselves, and only Describe() would show that.
The class knows slots, types, and defaults, but not the names of the inputs. The caller can still swap two inputs of the same type that sit next to each other, and Verify() would accept the result. The class can't tell an enum from an int, a datetime from a long, or a color from a uint, and it doesn't check an enum range.
Whether the last slot is an applied price has to be passed to Load(). I found no way to tell from the reply. A wrong flag shows up as one input too many or one too few in Describe().
Load() needs a handle created with the defaults. NeedsInputs showed that a refusal in OnInit() doesn't stop the layout from loading, but that is one indicator. An indicator whose handle can't be created with its defaults can't be loaded.
Tester support is partial. In the Strategy Tester the handle is not verified, because IndicatorParameters() is not allowed there. The tester relies on a layout file written earlier on a chart, and only SaveLayout.mq5, run outside the tester, can tell that the file is stale.
I tested custom indicators that take their inputs from iCustom() and IndicatorCreate() by value. I did not test indicators that receive another indicator's handle as their price source, indicators called on a custom symbol, or Market indicators. The two tables cover the listed values only.
crosscheck.py applies the rules from this article a second time. It checks the MQL5 results against a second implementation of the same rules, not against an outside reference.
Conclusion
On builds 6204 and 6230, every input group line in the five indicators I tested took a parameter slot in iCustom() and IndicatorCreate(). The documentation doesn't say so, and for numeric values the terminal didn't say so either. Within the tested values, a value that lands in the wrong numeric slot is accepted, and only a mix of strings and numbers gave error 4002. Some values change even in the right slot: integers wrap, floats round, and strings longer than 245 characters are cut. BandsLite called the obvious way ran for 9 months of EURUSD H1 with a period of 2 and produced no signal at all.
CIndicatorInputs reads the layout from a running indicator and probes which slots are groups or floats. It fills the group slots, refuses values the terminal would silently change, and checks the handle after it is made on a chart. For an EA that doesn't use the class, CallText() gives the same order as one ready iCustom() line. In the Strategy Tester, where IndicatorParameters() fails with error 4014, the class builds the handle from a layout file but can't verify it. SaveLayout.mq5 reports a stale file before the test.
The next part of the series looks at chart labels that stop at 63 characters without a warning.
To try it, unpack MQL5.zip into the terminal's data folder and compile the indicators first. Run TestIndicatorInputs.mq5, TypeMatrix.mq5, and ShiftCost.mq5 on a EURUSD H1 chart, and run SaveLayout.mq5 before testing GroupCallerEA.mq5. crosscheck.py reads the files they write to MQL5\Files\IcustomGroups.

Статья относится к категории 'MQL5 Developer Gotchas' — это техническое предупреждение для разработчиков, а не описание торговой системы.
judge.summary: Статья посвящена технической особенности MQL5: при вызове кастомных индикаторов с input group через iCustom() или IndicatorCreate() каждая строка группы занимает отдельный слот в параметрическом массиве, что приводит к сдвигу значений параметров, если пустые строки для групп не указаны явно. Автор демонстрирует последствия этого поведения на примере индикатора BandsLite и предлагает класс CIndicatorInputs для автоматического определения слотов и корректной передачи параметров.
